source.title: Membership Privacy Risks of Sharpness Aware Minimization
source.authors: Young In Kim; Andrea Agiollo; Pratik K. Agrawal; J. O. Royset; Rajiv Khanna

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices; no cut-off or garbling prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own SAM-versus-SGD results showing that better test accuracy can coexist with higher membership-inference success, qualifying the assumed link between generalization and privacy. It does not test the listed claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper compares test accuracy and membership-inference outcomes for SAM and SGD, and for other sharpness-aware optimizers. It does not measure train–test error gaps, random-label memorization, or the listed interventions and properties as specified in V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether SAM improves test accuracy while increasing membership leakage. None of V1–V8 predicts that relationship. Its memorization and influence analyses do not compare removing highly memorized examples with removing equally many random examples (V8), and its Hessian trace measurements do not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its association with generalization gaps (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' main conclusion: SAM can improve held-out accuracy while increasing membership leakage. They interpret memorization and influence analyses as evidence that SAM captures atypical informative subpatterns better. Their variance-reduction mechanism is established for an idealized curvature-aligned linear interpolation model under stated assumptions; its extension to practical SAM is an explanatory interpretation.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares SAM with SGD and sharpness-aware variants; it does not reproduce the claim's random-label, width, architecture, adaptive-optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness-measure, or example-removal experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset, attack method (direct threshold versus online/offline shadow models), and architecture; Texas-100 has a lower SAM TPR@.1% than SGD in the online table, while other attack measures there are higher.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM has higher test accuracy than SGD in the reported comparisons and generally higher membership-inference success, with some attack-specific exceptions and ties.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Better held-out accuracy under SAM can coexist with greater membership leakage.

fits_no_version.finding: Sections 4.1–4.3 report broader memorization under SAM, stronger influence of mid-to-high memorization samples, and greater SAM accuracy gains in atypical test buckets. SGD scores come from publicly available estimates; bucket membership differs between optimizers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM's accuracy gains are associated with greater reliance on atypical training patterns, as assessed through memorization and influence estimates.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the stated assumptions and sufficiently small positive geometry parameter, the linear interpolation analysis predicts reduced non-member output variance and increased confidence- and likelihood-ratio attack advantages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Curvature-aligned interpolation geometry can increase membership leakage through reduced non-member output variance.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 5 reports CIFAR-100 Hessian traces of 1556.54 for Sharp, 307.87 for SGD, and 84.18 for SAM; Table 3 reports corresponding optimizer differences in test accuracy and attack success.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These optimizer comparisons associate lower Hessian trace with higher test accuracy and generally greater membership leakage.

record.problems: The study does not report training error for the model comparisons, so the train–test generalization gap cannot be calculated from these tables. Some comparisons rely on publicly available SGD memorization and influence scores rather than retraining SGD in the study. Theoretical results depend on stated assumptions and sufficiently small η.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable V1–V8 results were omitted. Table 3's direct-threshold comparisons for Sharp, ASAM, and GSAM were not extracted because these additional optimizer rows would repeat the SAM/SGD optimizer comparison without testing any listed version; Table 3 remains available in the supplied text.

untested.parts: No comparison of fitting fixed random labels and generalizing on natural labels under the same architecture and recipe.
No width sweep beyond the width needed for zero training error.
No matched convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive-gradient versus SGD comparison under the specified tuning conditions. ASAM adapts sharpness perturbations and does not supply that comparison.
No within-workload batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted recipes.
No dropout intervention or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
No magnitude-aware perturbation-tolerance measurements, comparison of similarly low training losses and generalization gaps, or ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.

No removal of highly memorized training examples followed by retraining and comparison with equally sized random removals. Leave-one-out influence estimates and test-accuracy buckets do not establish this removal effect.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T5 classification is inconsistent with its correctly unlinked rows. Qualifying a generalization–privacy expectation does not qualify any supplied claim version. No V1–V8 verdict is warranted. The unrecorded memorization, bucket, and Hessian results concern adjacent claims, so they are described under fits_no_version rather than missing.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fit and natural-label generalization coexistence; no random-label training or chance-level test comparison.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
SAM is compared with SGD, but adaptive optimizers and the version's tuning, decay, switching, and language-model conditions are not tested.
The paper studies SAM's sharpness-related geometry, but does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or rank generalization gaps against norm- or margin-based measures.
No removal and retraining of memorized examples.

rows.subject: SAM and SGD
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical comparison of minimum-G interpolation with Euclidean geometry versus sharpness-aware geometry Gη = I + ηΣ.

conditions.value: Under Assumption 1 and sufficiently small η > 0

rows.measure: Variance of non-member outputs and confidence-based and likelihood-ratio MIA advantage
rows.baseline: Euclidean geometry G0
rows.value: For sufficiently small η > 0, non-member output variance strictly decreases and both attack advantages strictly increase with probability 1 − o(1).
rows.note: This is a theoretical result about generalization-related variance and membership risk, not a measured train–test error gap.
rows.check: The stated results match Theorems 1–3, but the subjects are minimum-norm linear interpolants under Euclidean and population-curvature geometries modeling SGD and SAM, rather than actual optimizer runs. Split variance and the two attack advantages into separate results.
